web_evidence.title: Teaching the Universe of Discourse, Chapter Four: Narrative: What Happened
web_evidence.note: An authorized excerpt from pages 286–287 of the novel is presented under “Anonymous Narration: Multiple Character Point of View”; the accompanying explanation describes an impersonal perspective extending beyond any one character.

web_evidence.title: Ship of Fools — Novels for Students
web_evidence.note: The point-of-view section explicitly identifies a third-person omniscient narrator who knows the characters’ thoughts and shifts focal perspective among them.

web_evidence.title: An Analysis of Katherine Anne Porter's Novel Ship of Fools
web_evidence.note: The scholarly analysis describes an episodic method that moves among passengers and groups and quotes Porter characterizing her authorial position as distributed throughout the cast, corroborating external multiple-character narration.

web_evidence.title: Some Observations on the Genesis of “Ship of Fools”: A Letter from Katherine Anne Porter
web_evidence.note: The PMLA note establishes that Porter's voyage diary supplied source notes for fiction drafted later; it does not indicate that the published novel is diary or epistolary narration.

search_log: Searched “Katherine Anne Porter Ship of Fools excerpt first chapter” and the Google Books preview; the publisher listing verified the edition and cast but exposed no sustained prose in the crawler, so it was not used as person evidence.

Searched “Ship of Fools narrator point of view third person omniscient” and opened the Encyclopedia.com and GradeSaver point-of-view pages; Encyclopedia.com supplied the stronger explicit whole-book description.

Searched scholarly combinations including “Ship of Fools Porter narrative technique narrator,” “omniscient,” and “narrative point of view”; opened the authorized WAC excerpt and Ball State scholarly analysis.

Searched specifically for epistolary, diary, frame-narrative, multiple-narrator, and alternating-narration claims; the PMLA genesis note showed that the diary was source material, and no credible source described sustained first- or second-person base sections.
person_note: The controlling narrator is an anonymous nonparticipant who narrates the cast in third person while moving among characters’ private thoughts. Quotes q01167, q01170, q01171, q01174, and q01176 independently display that pattern, agreeing with the authorized interior excerpt and whole-book structural sources. Visible I, we, and you forms occur in dialogue, gnomic statements, or free-direct character thought rather than autonomous base-narrative sections. Porter's real voyage diary was source material, not the novel's constitutive narration. No material contrary evidence remains.
